flawed_step: The parenthetical assumes that the graph obtained by contracting the triangle can be 3-edge-coloured. It is again a bridgeless cubic graph, but it need not be colourable: it can be the Petersen graph. Colourability passes both ways between the two graphs, so a triangle gives no help.
counterexample: Take the Petersen graph P and a vertex v with neighbours a, b, c. Replace v by a triangle x, y, z with edges xy, yz, zx, xa, yb, zc. The resulting graph G is simple, cubic and bridgeless, since P is 3-edge-connected and replacing a vertex by a triangle keeps G at least 2-edge-connected. G contains the triangle xyz. Suppose G had a 3-edge-colouring. The triangle edges must get three different colours, say xy=1, yz=2, zx=3. Then at each triangle vertex the outgoing edge gets the missing colour: xa=2, yb=3, zc=1, all different. Contracting the triangle back to v then gives a proper 3-edge-colouring of the Petersen graph, which is impossible. So G is a bridgeless cubic graph with a triangle and no 3-edge-colouring.
assessment_summary: False. Replacing one vertex of the Petersen graph by a triangle gives a 12-vertex simple bridgeless cubic graph with a triangle. Any 3-edge-colouring of it would force distinct colours on the three edges leaving the triangle, so contracting the triangle would 3-edge-colour the Petersen graph, which is impossible.
